summary: A snapshot of the standardization state of protocols used in the Internet as of October 2, 2003. It lists official protocol standards and Best Current Practice RFCs and is not a complete index. It was designated STD 1. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 3700.

eli5.summary: This is a list showing which rules had official status on one day in 2003. Later editions replaced it, so it is only history now.

subtitle: A snapshot of official Internet protocols and standards from 2003

tldr.problem: Internet administrators and developers need a reference showing which protocols have official standardization status and where they fit in the standards maturity process.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC lists all protocols approved through the IETF standardization process as of October 2, 2003, organized by status level (Standard, Draft Standard, Proposed Standard, Experimental) and by both protocol name and RFC number.
tldr.outcome: The Internet Standards documentation becomes dynamic: newer versions of this snapshot are published regularly as the standards process evolves, with this 2003 version being superseded by RFC 3700 and later editions.

today: RFC 3600 is Historic. It has been superseded by RFC 3700 (2004) and later editions. The living, authoritative list of Internet Official Protocol Standards is now maintained at the RFC Editor website, updated daily, rather than in a single RFC document.

sections.title: Introduction and Overview
sections.content:
RFC 3600 is a formal reference document designated STD 1, the standard listing of Internet protocol standards. It contains a snapshot of the standardization state of all protocols used in the Internet as of October 2, 2003, capturing the output of the IETF standardization process up to that date.

The RFC is organized into seven sections of protocol listings (sections 3.1 through 3.7), each representing a different maturity level in the IETF standards track. Protocols marked with an asterisk indicate changes from the previous version of this document.
sections.eli5: This document is like a year-end school report showing which students passed, which are still testing, and which are experimental. It's a snapshot from one day, and a new one comes out when things change.

sections.title: Document Scope and Purpose
sections.content:
This memo contains a comprehensive but not exhaustive list. It focuses on officially standardized protocols, Best Current Practice (BCP) documents, and Experimental protocols that have gone through IETF review. Informational and Historic RFCs are not included in this listing.

The document is published by the RFC Editor for the Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG) and Internet Architecture Board (IAB) in accordance with RFC 2026, which defines the rules and procedures for setting Internet standards. Each protocol entry includes its mnemonic, full title, RFC number, and standardization level or STD number.
sections.eli5: The document shows which rules are 'official Internet standard,' which ones are 'draft' (almost ready), which are 'just ideas,' and which are 'experiments.' Old rules that don't work anymore are not listed here.

sections.title: Protocol Categories and Status Levels
sections.content:
The RFC organizes protocols into six main categories based on their standards status. Standard Protocols have completed the entire IETF review and approval process and are listed both by their assigned STD number and by RFC number. Draft Standard Protocols are nearly complete, having demonstrated implementation and operational experience. Proposed Standard Protocols are undergoing review to determine if they meet requirements for wider standardization.

Best Current Practice (BCP) documents describe operational and administrative practices rather than protocol specifications, and also receive official approval. Experimental Protocols represent technically interesting ideas that may not be ready for standardization. Each category reflects how mature and widely adopted the specification is within the Internet community.
sections.eli5: Protocols are ranked like school grades: 'Standard' means it's official, 'Draft Standard' means it's almost official, 'Proposed' means it's being tested, 'Experimental' means someone just had an idea, and 'Best Current Practice' means it's how we actually operate networks.

sections.title: Using This Document to Find Resources
sections.content:
The document provides multiple access paths to the RFC repository. It explains how to retrieve protocols via FTP from ftp.rfc-editor.org using the file naming convention in-notes/rfcnnnn.txt (where nnnn is the unpadded RFC number). It also describes an email-based query service (RFC-INFO@RFC-EDITOR.ORG) that allows administrators to request RFCs and search them by author, title, or keyword.

The RFC references RFC 2026 for detailed understanding of the Internet Standards Process and directs readers to http://www.rfc-editor.org for the living, daily-updated version of this standards list, as the printed version becomes out of date as new protocols are standardized.
sections.eli5: The document tells you how to find these rulebooks. You can download them, email for them, or look them up on a website that updates every day with new rules.

sections.title: The Evolution of Standards Documentation
sections.content:
RFC 3600 is the third major revision of STD 1, following RFC 3300 (2002) and earlier versions. This document is intentionally temporary by design—it is meant to be superseded by newer editions as the standards process produces new approved specifications. The RFC explicitly states that the authoritative, always-current version of the Internet Official Protocol Standards is maintained on the RFC Editor's website and updated daily.

This snapshot captures protocols from the early 2000s, including foundational protocols like TCP (RFC 793), IP (RFC 791), and UDP (RFC 768), alongside emerging technologies like IPv6 (RFC 2460) and SNMPv3 (RFC 3413). Historic protocols that are no longer used are explicitly marked as such rather than being completely omitted, preserving the historical record.
sections.eli5: This document is like a photo from 2003 showing the rulebooks that existed then. Technology moves on, so newer photos (RFCs) replace it, but it's useful to see what was official at one moment in time.
